newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco to enlarge banks forex activities.
newsitem.headline: Morocco to enlarge banks forex activities.

text.p: Morocco, in a move aimed at speeding up liberalisation of forex market, will soon allow local banks to exchange hard currencies with foreign financial institutions, Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj said on Tuesday.

Kabbaj told the national council of money and saving that the indicators for the past year were very positive and encouraged the government to pursue its financial reforms to upgrade the country's economy.

"Morocco's economy registered a double-digit growth to 11.8 percent in 1996 from 6.7 percent in 1995...The deficit was halved to 3.0 percent and the current account was cut to 1.2 percent from 4.6 percent in 1995," Kabbaj said.

Kabbaj, who held an ordinary meeting with the governor of Bank al-Maghrib (central bank) and leaders of commercial banks said "the authorities agreed to enlarge the forex market activities and allow the banks to exchange hard currencies directly with foreign banks."
In past years, the banks needed central bank permission to exchange currencies with foreign financial institutions.
Kabbaj gave no date for the implementation of the government's decision.
He said the monetary authorities were examining the set up of a central depository body for the Casablanca stock exchange as part of the ongoing reforms launched in 1993.
"The central depository body will be operational in the fourth quarter of 1997," Kabbaj told the meeting.
Morocco also plans to set up "a second market" for trading small growing companies, the minister said.

According to Moroccan law, a minimum of 15 million dirhams ($1.66 million) are needed to introduce a firm on the the Casablanca stock echange, a broker said. "Most of the country's 6,000 companies do not possess that amount of money...This is why the government want create a second market..," he added.
Established in 1929, the Casablanca bourse has 47 listed stocks, including eight banks.
Kabbaj also disclosed that a project of launching a "rating agency" for the Moroccan foreign debt "was underway with international institutions and would be set up soon."
The minister gave no other details.
Morocco's total foreign debt is estimated at $22 billion, officials said.
A Casablanca-based market analyst said U.S. JP Morgan institution is negotiating the deal with Morocco to choose the "rating agency."
Kabbaj urged the commercial banks to "react to signals sent by the monetary authorities at the end of 1996 in order to reduce their interest rates to boost the economic growth."
Bank al-Maghrib cut by half a point to 6.5 percent interest rates on the weekly repurchase auctions but the bank have little enthusiasm since.
